qs.q: Which clotting factor is deficient in Haemophilia A?
qs.e: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII. (Haemophilia B, by contrast, is a deficiency of Factor IX.)
qs.s: Haematology Exam MCQs: Anemia, Leukemia, Coagulation Prep — Hematopathology III

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Haemophilia is an X‑linked deficiency of clotting factor VIII (type A) or IX (type B) causing prolonged bleeding. Diagnosis relies on coagulation studies and factor assays.

sections.p: A hereditary bleeding disorder due to reduced activity of factor VIII (HA) or IX (HB). Diagnosis requires a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with normal PT, followed by specific factor activity assays.
b: Factor VIII or IX activity <30% confirms diagnosis

t.b: Is intrinsic pathway prolonged? → Yes suggests factor VIII/IX deficiency; normal PT rules out extrinsic defects.
What is the specific factor level? → <30% confirms haemophilia; >30% suggests mild disease or carrier.
Does patient plasma correct aPTT when mixed with normal plasma? → No correction indicates inhibitor presence.

sections.p: Severity is classified by factor activity: severe <1%, moderate 1–5%, mild 5–40%. Severity predicts spontaneous joint bleeds and need for prophylaxis.
b: Mild: bleeding only with surgery or major injury

sections.p: Most cases are inherited X‑linked recessive mutations in F8 (HA) or F9 (HB). Acquired inhibitors can develop after repeated exposure to factor concentrates, especially in low‑resource settings where plasma products are used.
b: Rare autosomal recessive combined factor deficiencies

sections.p: Patients present with prolonged bleeding after minor cuts, easy bruising, hemarthroses (especially knees, elbows), and deep muscle bleeds. In infants, prolonged umbilical stump bleeding is a clue.
Coagulation screening guides further testing; factor assays quantify deficiency; inhibitor screens detect antibodies that neutralise replacement therapy.

t.b: Is an inhibitor present? → Positive (>0.6 BU) means bypassing agents needed.
Is there anemia from chronic bleeding? → Low Hb supports ongoing loss.
Is there joint effusion? → Confirms hemarthrosis, guides physiotherapy.

sections.p: Life‑threatening bleeding includes intracranial hemorrhage, massive gastrointestinal bleed, and compartment syndrome from muscle bleeds. Chronic joint disease (hemophilic arthropathy) leads to disability.
b: Severe head trauma with loss of consciousness

sections.p: Replace the missing factor using plasma‑derived or recombinant concentrates; use bypassing agents (e.g., activated prothrombin complex) if inhibitors are present. Supportive care includes antifibrinolytics for mucosal bleeds and physiotherapy for joints.
b: Factor VIII or IX concentrate for on‑demand bleed control
Prophylactic regular dosing in severe disease
Avoid fresh frozen plasma when inhibitors likely
Tranexamic acid for dental or minor mucosal bleeds

sections.p: Regular monitoring of factor levels, inhibitor screening, and joint assessment are essential. Vaccination against hepatitis B and C reduces infection risk from plasma products. Education on injury avoidance is crucial.
Other bleeding disorders that also prolong aPTT or cause bruising.
b: Von Willebrand disease (normal factor VIII in mild cases)

sections.p: Mild haemophilia may have near‑normal aPTT, and early inhibitor development can give falsely normal factor levels if not specifically tested.
b: Normal aPTT in mild disease → missed diagnosis
Low inhibitor titre missed without Bethesda assay

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache or loss of consciousness (possible intracranial bleed)
Unexplained abdominal pain with distension (possible intra‑abdominal bleed)
Rapidly expanding joint swelling with severe pain

faq.q: Why is PT usually normal in haemophilia?
faq.a: PT measures the extrinsic pathway, which does not involve factor VIII or IX.
Rarely, as carriers with skewed X‑inactivation or homozygous females can manifest disease.

faq.q: What is the role of antifibrinolytics?
faq.a: They stabilize clots in mucosal surfaces and reduce bleeding when factor replacement is not needed.
